profile.feeling: The speaker; small and unstressed, never capitalized except at the start of a sentence.

senses.def: I (the speaker); mich = me (accusative), mir = (to) me (dative)
das Ich: the self, the ego (used as a noun)

phrases.meaning: the usual answer when someone asks who is there

profile.synonymsNone: A personal pronoun has no synonyms; only its case forms change (ich, mich, mir, meiner).

etymology.text: From Middle High German ich, from Old High German ih, from Proto-West Germanic *ik, from Proto-Germanic *ek, *ik, from Proto-Indo-European *eǵh₂óm.

funFacts: Freud's “Ego” is das Ich in the German original: Das Ich und das Es (“The Ego and the Id”, 1923).
pitfalls: ich is written lower-case inside a sentence – unlike English “I”.
Pick the case: ich (subject), mich (direct object: Er sieht mich), mir (indirect object or after a dative preposition: mit mir).
subtleties: “It's me” is Ich bin's / Ich bin es – the verb agrees with ich, not with es.

profile.feeling: Closeness and equality: family, friends, children, young people, many workplaces and the internet.

senses.def: you (one person you know well – informal address); dich = you (accusative), dir = (to) you (dative)
you (generic, “one”) in casual speech: Da weißt du nie, was passiert.

examples.text: Ich rufe dich heute Abend an.
Mama, ich habe dir Blumen gekauft.
In dem Job weißt du nie, was am nächsten Tag passiert.
examples.tr: In that job you never know what will happen the next day.

phrases.tr: Shall we say du to each other?
phrases.meaning: the polite question that ends Sie-address between adults

synonyms.nuance: the polite “you” for adults you do not know well, at work, in shops and offices; takes the verb forms of the 3rd person plural

etymology.text: From Middle High German du, duo, dū, from Old High German dū (akin to Old Saxon thū and English thou), from Proto-West Germanic *þū, from Proto-Germanic *þū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂.

funFacts: German has verbs for it: duzen (to say du) and siezen (to say Sie).
Traditionally, switching from Sie to du was sealed with a drink: Brüderschaft trinken.
pitfalls: Using du with a stranger, a shop assistant or an official can sound rude; the older or higher-ranking person usually offers the du.
Verb ending -st: du isst, du trinkst, du bist, du hast.
subtleties: In letters and e-mails du/dich/dir may be capitalized (Du, Dich, Dir) as a sign of respect; both spellings are correct.
Many companies, start-ups and online services address everyone with du; IKEA in Germany famously does.

profile.feeling: Respectful distance: strangers, customers, officials, teachers, older people.

senses.def: you (polite address to one person) – always capitalized; Ihnen = (to) you (dative)
you (polite address to several people)

examples.tr: What would you like to drink? (lit. What are you drinking?)

examples.text: Frau Müller, haben Sie einen Moment Zeit?
examples.tr: Ms Müller, do you have a moment?

examples.text: Meine Damen und Herren, ich danke Ihnen für Ihre Aufmerksamkeit.
examples.tr: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your attention.

phrases.meaning: the formal greeting question; informal: Wie geht's dir?

synonyms.nuance: the familiar “you” for one person: family, friends, children, peers

etymology.text: The same word as sie “they”: because the polite form uses the 3rd person plural, the pronoun began to be capitalized in the 17th century to distinguish the form of address from “they”.

funFacts: Polite Sie is grammatically “they”: Sie essen means both “you eat” (polite) and “they eat” – only the capital letter tells them apart in writing.
pitfalls: Always capitalize Sie, Ihnen (and Ihr = your) when they mean polite “you”; sie with a small s means “she” or “they”.
The verb takes the 3rd person plural form: Sie sind, Sie haben, Sie essen – never *Sie bist.
subtleties: Sie is used for one person and for several people alike.

profile.feeling: A man or boy – and any thing whose noun is masculine (der Kürbis → er).

senses.def: he (a male person); ihn = him (accusative), ihm = (to) him (dative)
it – for any noun with the article der (der Kohl → er)

examples.text: Ich kenne ihn seit der Schule.
Wo ist der Knoblauch? – Er liegt im Schrank.
examples.tr: Where's the garlic? – It's in the cupboard.

synonyms.nuance: stressed demonstrative used for people in casual speech (Der kommt nicht.); can sound dismissive

etymology.text: From Middle High German ër, from Old High German ër, from Proto-West Germanic *iʀ, from Proto-Germanic *iz. The spelling ih- in ihm, ihn was introduced in early modern German to keep them apart from im, in.

funFacts: The h in ihn and ihm is not pronounced; it was added in writing only to distinguish them from in and im.
pitfalls: Things are er when their noun is masculine: Der Salat ist frisch – er ist frisch (not *es).
Accusative ihn vs dative ihm: Ich sehe ihn. / Ich helfe ihm.
subtleties: In casual speech Germans often say der instead of er for people (Der ist nett.) – neutral among friends, but it can sound disrespectful about someone present.

profile.feeling: A woman or girl – and any thing whose noun is feminine (die Tomate → sie).

senses.def: she (a female person); sie = her (accusative), ihr = (to) her (dative)
it – for any noun with the article die (die Gurke → sie)

examples.text: Wo ist die Gurke? – Sie ist im Kühlschrank.
examples.tr: Where's the cucumber? – It's in the fridge.

synonyms.nuance: stressed demonstrative used for people in casual speech (Die kommt gleich.); can sound dismissive

etymology.text: From Middle High German siu, si, from Old High German siu, si, from Proto-West Germanic *si(j)u, *sī, from Proto-Germanic *sī. Cognate with Gothic 𐍃𐌹 (si).

funFacts: sie has three meanings in German: she, they – and, capitalized, the polite you (Sie).
pitfalls: sie (she) and sie (they) look the same; the verb tells them apart: sie isst (she) / sie essen (they).
Dative is ihr, not *sie: Ich helfe ihr.
subtleties: Feminine things are sie too: die Kartoffel → sie. A girl (das Mädchen) is grammatically neuter (es), but in everyday speech people often refer to her with sie.

profile.feeling: Togetherness: the family, the team, the group – and sometimes the whole country.

senses.def: we; uns = us (accusative and dative)

examples.text: Wir kaufen Gemüse auf dem Markt.
examples.tr: We buy vegetables at the market.
Will you visit us at the weekend?

collocations.tr: at our place; where we live

phrases.meaning: a famous headline of the Bild newspaper (2005) when the German Joseph Ratzinger became pope; now a joking pattern for national pride

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; in colloquial speech man can replace wir (Man geht jetzt. = We're going now).

etymology.text: From Middle High German wir, from Old High German wir, from Proto-West Germanic *wiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *wīz, from Proto-Indo-European *wéy. Compare Dutch wij, English we, Danish vi.

funFacts: The verb form after wir is the same as the infinitive for almost every verb: wir essen, wir kaufen, wir trinken – the exception is sein: wir sind.
pitfalls: uns is both accusative and dative: Er sieht uns. / Er hilft uns.
subtleties: bei uns means “at our home” or “in our country/region”, depending on context.

profile.feeling: Other people – or several things of any gender.

senses.def: they; sie = them (accusative), ihnen = (to) them (dative)
they/them for things – any plural noun, whatever its gender (die Kartoffeln → sie)

examples.text: Die Tomaten sind reif, wir können sie pflücken.
examples.tr: The tomatoes are ripe; we can pick them.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; in casual speech the demonstrative die is often used for people (Die kommen später.).

etymology.text: From Middle High German sie, si, from Old High German sie (masculine plural), sio (feminine plural), siu (neuter plural).

funFacts: Capitalize it and it becomes the polite “you”: sie essen (they eat) – Sie essen (you eat).
pitfalls: ihnen (to them) vs Ihnen (to you, polite): only the capital letter differs.
The verb is plural: sie essen (they), but sie isst (she).
subtleties: One plural pronoun for everything: German makes no gender difference in the plural.

profile.feeling: The most basic verb: who and what something is, where it is, how it is.

senses.def: to be (identity, quality, place): Das ist eine Tomate. Der Salat ist frisch. Wo ist die Gurke?
auxiliary of the perfect for verbs of motion and change: Ich bin gegangen.
to exist, to be alive
to be someone's turn (in a game, in a queue)

examples.text: Die Kartoffeln sind noch zu hart.
examples.tr: The potatoes are still too hard.

examples.text: Wo bist du? Ich bin schon im Restaurant.
examples.tr: Where are you? I'm already at the restaurant.

examples.text: Wir sind gestern nach Berlin gefahren.
Wer ist jetzt dran? – Du bist dran!
examples.tr: Whose turn is it? – It's your turn!

collocations.tr: to be there, to be present

phrases.text: Sein oder Nichtsein, das ist hier die Frage.
phrases.tr: To be or not to be, that is the question.
phrases.meaning: Hamlet's famous line in the classic German translation
phrases.source: Shakespeare, Hamlet III.1, German translation by August Wilhelm Schlegel (1798), public domain

phrases.tr: I'm cold. (lit. To me it is cold.)
phrases.meaning: how you feel: the person goes in the dative; Ich bin kalt means “I am a cold person”

particleVerbs.tr: to be present (written as two words)

synonyms.nuance: to be located – official or written style (Das Büro befindet sich im 2. Stock.)
to exist – philosophical or technical, not for location or qualities

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German sīn, from Old High German sīn, from Proto-West Germanic *sīn, an analogical infinitive within the suppletive paradigm of “to be” built on Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- (“to be, exist”); it replaced the older infinitive wesan (*wesaną “to be, remain”), and forms from *beuną (“to be, exist, become”) also enter the paradigm. Cognate with Dutch zijn.

funFacts: The paradigm mixes old roots: ist/sind (like Latin est, sunt), bin/bist (like English be), war/gewesen (from old wesan, like English was).
pitfalls: Feelings of cold, heat or sickness use the dative: Mir ist kalt / Mir ist schlecht. Ich bin kalt means “I am cold-hearted”.
Perfect with sein, not haben, for motion and change of state: Ich bin gefahren / Er ist gewesen.
subtleties: sein is also the possessive “his”/“its” (sein Buch) – a different word with the same spelling.

profile.feeling: Possession, but also everyday states: hunger, time, fear, luck.

senses.def: to have, to own, to possess
to have (a state or feeling): Hunger, Durst, Angst, Zeit, Glück haben
auxiliary of the perfect: Ich habe gegessen.

examples.text: Ich habe eine Gurke und zwei Tomaten.
examples.tr: I have a cucumber and two tomatoes.

examples.text: Er hat den ganzen Kuchen gegessen.
examples.tr: He has eaten the whole cake.

phrases.meaning: a shrugging, often ironic remark about someone who has (or can afford) what others do not

particleVerbs.tr: to have homework; to wear (a hat)

synonyms.nuance: to own, possess – legal or written style, only for ownership
to have at one's disposal – official style

etymology.text: From Middle High German haben, from Old High German habēn, from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to grasp”). Cognates include Dutch hebben, English have, Danish have.

funFacts: German “has” hunger, thirst, fear and luck where English “is” hungry, thirsty, afraid and lucky.
pitfalls: du hast, er hat – the b disappears in these two forms.
Age is said with sein, not haben: Ich bin 20 (Jahre alt), never *Ich habe 20 Jahre.
subtleties: Wir haben Montag / Wir haben Mai: “it is Monday / it is May” – haben for the date.
“There is/are” is es gibt, not haben (except regionally).

profile.feeling: Everyday and warm: shared meals (zusammen essen) are a social ritual.

senses.def: to eat (of people)
to have a meal, to dine (essen gehen = to eat out)

examples.text: Er isst jeden Tag einen Apfel.
examples.tr: He eats an apple every day.

examples.text: Wir essen um sieben Uhr zu Abend.

examples.tr: At the weekend we go out to eat.

phrases.meaning: How food looks matters.

phrases.text: Es wird nichts so heiß gegessen, wie es gekocht wird.
phrases.tr: Nothing is eaten as hot as it is cooked.
phrases.meaning: Things are rarely as bad as they first seem.

phrases.text: So jemand nicht will arbeiten, der soll auch nicht essen.
phrases.tr: If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat.
phrases.meaning: Who does not work should not eat.

particleVerbs.tr: to eat up, finish one's food
to eat with others, join in

synonyms.nuance: elevated “to dine”: restaurants, menus, ceremonies
to ingest, take (food) – medical or official language
to tuck in, eat heartily – playful
neutral for animals; said of people it means eating greedily, like an animal

etymology.text: From Middle High German ëȥȥen, from Old High German ëȥȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *etan, from Proto-Germanic *etaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-. Cognate with Dutch eten, English eat, Swedish äta; non-Germanic cognates include Latin edō and Russian есть (jestʹ).

funFacts: Animals do not “essen” in German, they “fressen” – using fressen for a person is rude or jokey.
The past participle is gegessen, with an extra -ge-; the old form gessen is obsolete.
pitfalls: Stem vowel e → i: du isst, er isst (not *esst); du isst and er isst are spelled the same.
Past tense with ß: ich aß, wir aßen.
subtleties: Soup is eaten in German (Suppe essen), not drunk.

profile.feeling: Coffee breaks, beer gardens, toasts – and, without an object, the drinking of alcohol.

senses.def: to drink (a liquid)
to drink alcohol (habitually) – used without an object: Er trinkt.
auf jemanden/etwas trinken: to drink to, to toast

examples.text: Was trinkst du? – Ein Wasser, bitte.
examples.tr: What are you drinking? – A water, please.
In the morning I always drink tea.

examples.text: Sein Vater trinkt seit Jahren nicht mehr.
examples.tr: His father hasn't drunk alcohol for years.
Let's drink to the bride and groom!

collocations.tr: to drink coffee (also: to have a coffee break)
to drink a glass of water

phrases.meaning: a toast

particleVerbs.tr: to raise one's glass to someone

synonyms.nuance: to slurp, sip noisily
to take a tiny sip
neutral for animals; for people: to drink a lot, especially alcohol – crude

etymology.text: From Middle High German trinken, from Old High German trinkan (attested since the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *drinkan. Cognates include Dutch drinken, English drink, Swedish dricka and Gothic 𐌳𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌺𐌰𐌽 (drigkan).

funFacts: Kaffee und Kuchen: in Germany “Kaffee trinken” in the afternoon is a small meal with cake, not just a drink.
pitfalls: Without an object, Er trinkt usually means “he drinks (too much alcohol)”.
Strong verb: trinken – trank – getrunken (not *getrinkt).
subtleties: Wollen wir einen Kaffee trinken gehen? is an invitation to meet and talk, not only to drink coffee.

profile.feeling: Shops, markets, the Saturday shopping list.

senses.def: to buy, to purchase
to buy (something) for someone: jemandem etwas kaufen

examples.text: Ich kaufe Gemüse immer auf dem Markt.
examples.tr: I always buy vegetables at the market.

examples.text: Wo hast du die Schuhe gekauft?
examples.tr: Where did you buy the shoes?

examples.text: Wir kaufen unserer Tochter ein Fahrrad.
examples.tr: We're buying our daughter a bicycle.

phrases.tr: to buy the cat in the sack
phrases.meaning: to buy something without having seen it (English: to buy a pig in a poke)

phrases.text: Das kaufe ich dir nicht ab.
phrases.tr: I'm not buying that from you.
phrases.meaning: I don't believe you

particleVerbs.tr: to buy from someone; (colloquial) to believe

synonyms.nuance: to acquire – contracts, official texts
to get, fetch – focus on obtaining, not on paying
to go shopping (for fun) – an anglicism

etymology.text: From Middle High German koufen, from Old High German koufōn, from Proto-West Germanic *kaupōn, an early borrowing of Latin caupō (“innkeeper, petty trader”). Related to English cheap and Swedish köpa.

funFacts: The Danish cognate is in Copenhagen: København = “merchants' harbour”.
pitfalls: einkaufen is “to go shopping” in general; kaufen needs an object: Ich kaufe Brot. / Ich gehe einkaufen.
subtleties: Kauf mir was! – with a dative, kaufen means buying for someone.

profile.feeling: Liking food, music, people – friendly, not passionate.

senses.def: to like (something or someone)
would like (in the form möchte, Konjunktiv II)
may (concession or possibility): Das mag sein.

examples.text: Ich mag Tomaten, aber keine Gurken.
examples.tr: I like tomatoes, but not cucumbers.

examples.text: Das mag sein, aber ich glaube es nicht.
examples.tr: That may be, but I don't believe it.

collocations.tr: not to like something at all

phrases.meaning: a concession: that may well be true (but …)

synonyms.nuance: to be fond of (a person) – warmer than mögen
to love – much stronger for people; for things it is emphatic (Ich liebe Pizza!)
mostly negated: Ich kann ihn nicht leiden = I can't stand him

etymology.text: From Middle High German mugen, from Old High German mugan, from Proto-West Germanic *magan, from Proto-Germanic *maganą, from Proto-Indo-European *megʰ-. Compare Dutch mogen, English may. The sense “to like” developed in the 16th century from negated nicht mögen (“not to be able to” → “not to like doing”); the old sense “to be able to” fell out of use in the 17th century.

funFacts: mögen is a cousin of English may and might: it once meant “to be able”.
pitfalls: For activities German prefers gern + verb: Ich schwimme gern (I like swimming), rather than Ich mag schwimmen.
No ending in ich mag / er mag; vowel change ö → a in the singular.
subtleties: Ich mag dich (I like you) – Ich hab dich lieb (I'm fond of you, family and friends) – Ich liebe dich (I love you).
möchte (would like) is the polite way to ask for something; Ich will … can sound demanding.

profile.feeling: Direct will and intention – honest, but can sound blunt in a shop.

senses.def: to want (something or to do something)
to claim (Er will es nicht gewusst haben = he claims not to have known)
to be about to, to intend

examples.text: Die Kinder wollen heute Pizza essen.
examples.tr: The children want to eat pizza today.

examples.text: Er will nichts davon gewusst haben.
examples.tr: He claims to have known nothing about it.

examples.text: Ich wollte gerade gehen, als du angerufen hast.
examples.tr: I was just about to leave when you called.

phrases.text: Wer nicht will, der hat schon.
phrases.meaning: if you turn down an offer, that's your loss

particleVerbs.tr: to want to come along (colloquial: Willst du mit?)

synonyms.nuance: would like – the polite choice when asking for something
to wish, desire – service language: Was wünschen Sie?
to feel like (doing) something

etymology.text: From Middle High German wollen, wöllen, wellen, from Old High German wollen, wellen, from a blend of Proto-West Germanic *willjan and *walljan, from Proto-Germanic *wiljaną and *waljaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-. Compare Dutch willen, English will.

funFacts: English “will” was once “to want”, too – that sense survives in “if you will” and in “willing”.
pitfalls: False friend: German Ich will = I want, not “I will”. The future is werden: Ich werde kommen.
Ich will einen Kaffee can sound rude when ordering – say Ich möchte … or Ich hätte gern …
subtleties: Like other modal verbs, wollen often drops a verb of motion: Ich will nach Hause. Willst du mit?

profile.feeling: Agreement and confirmation; as a little modal word, “as you know”.

senses.def: yes (answer to a question)
modal particle: as we know, after all, obviously (Das ist ja toll!)

examples.tr: Do you like tomatoes? – Yes, very much!

phrases.meaning: to say “I do” – to marry someone

synonyms.nuance: emphatic “yes, sir” – military or very deferential; also ironic
exactly, right – agreement in conversation
yes – but ONLY as the answer that contradicts a negative question or statement

etymology.text: From Middle High German ja, from Old High German ja, jā (“yes”), from Proto-Germanic *ja (“yes”). Cognate with Yiddish יאָ (yo).

funFacts: The famous unstressed ja in the middle of sentences (Du bist ja nass!) is one of the German modal particles that have no direct English equivalent.
pitfalls: Answering a negative question with ja is ambiguous: Magst du keine Tomaten? – Doch! (Yes, I do.) / Nein. (No, I don't.)
subtleties: Mid-sentence, unstressed ja is not “yes” but a modal particle that marks something as obvious or surprising.

profile.feeling: A clear refusal or denial – softened with danke.

senses.def: no (answer to a question)
exclamation of surprise or disbelief (Nein, wirklich?)

examples.text: Willst du noch Kaffee? – Nein, danke.
examples.tr: Do you want more coffee? – No, thank you.

examples.text: Nein, das ist keine Gurke, das ist eine Zucchini.
examples.tr: No, that's not a cucumber, it's a zucchini.

examples.text: Nein! Wirklich? Das glaube ich nicht.
examples.tr: No! Really? I don't believe it.

phrases.meaning: a refusal must be respected

synonyms.nuance: relaxed spoken “nope”, very common in northern and central Germany
casual, slightly cheeky “nah”

etymology.text: From Middle High German nein, from a contraction of Old High German ni ein (“not one”). Compare Old English nān, from ne ān (Modern English none, further contracted to no).

funFacts: nein literally means “not one” – the same pattern as English none (ne + one).
pitfalls: nein answers a question; inside a sentence the negation is nicht or kein: Ich mag keine Zwiebeln (not *Ich mag nein Zwiebeln).
subtleties: To contradict a negative statement you say doch, not ja: Du magst keinen Spinat. – Doch!

profile.feeling: The everyday negation of verbs, adjectives and whole statements.

senses.def: not (negates a verb, an adjective, an adverb or a definite noun phrase)
nicht? / nicht wahr? – tag question “isn't it?, right?”

examples.text: Du kommst doch morgen, nicht wahr?

phrases.meaning: quite good – a typical German understatement of praise

synonyms.nuance: colloquial pronunciation in Austria and southern Germany
spoken form, especially in northern Germany

etymology.text: From Middle High German niwiht, niweht, niht, a contracted form of Old High German niowiht, from Proto-West Germanic *naiwwiht; essentially nio (“never”) + wiht (“being, creature, thing”) – literally “not a thing”.

funFacts: English not has the same history: from Old English nāwiht “no thing” (also the source of naught).
pitfalls: nicht vs kein: kein replaces “not a / not any” before a noun without the definite article (Ich habe keine Gurke), nicht negates verbs, adjectives and nouns with der/die/das (Ich esse die Gurke nicht).
Position: nicht usually comes after the object and at the end of a main clause (Ich mag ihn nicht), but before adjectives, places and second verbs (nicht frisch, nicht hier, nicht essen).
subtleties: The position of nicht can change what is negated: Ich esse nicht die Gurke (but something else) vs Ich esse die Gurke nicht (not at all).

profile.feeling: “None at all”: the negative article that replaces ein and plurals without an article.

senses.def: no, not a, not any (negates a noun that would have ein or no article)
keiner / keine / keins (as a pronoun): nobody, none

phrases.meaning: I don't know (at all)
that's not surprising

synonyms.nuance: “not one” – only with emphasis on the number: Nicht ein Gast ist gekommen

etymology.text: From Middle High German kein, a back-formation from original nekein (“not any”), from Old High German nihein, from Proto-West Germanic *nehwain, from Proto-Germanic *nehw ainaz (“not any”). Compare Dutch geen, Yiddish קיין (keyn).

funFacts: kein is declined exactly like ein in the singular – but unlike ein it has a plural: keine Tomaten.
pitfalls: *Ich habe nicht eine Tomate is not the normal negation – say Ich habe keine Tomate.
kein takes the case endings of ein: keinen Kürbis (masc. accusative), keiner Gurke (fem. dative).
subtleties: Used alone as a pronoun it takes adjective-like endings: Hast du einen Apfel? – Nein, ich habe keinen.

profile.feeling: The glue of every list and story.

senses.def: and (joins words, phrases and sentences)
Und? / Na und? – so? so what? (colloquial question)

examples.text: Er kocht, und sie deckt den Tisch.
examples.tr: He cooks and she sets the table.

examples.text: Ich habe keine Zeit. – Na und?
examples.tr: I have no time. – So what?

phrases.meaning: I don't care / why does that matter?

synonyms.nuance: as well as – written, often in lists
plus, and also

etymology.text: From Middle High German unde, from Old High German unti, from Proto-Germanic *andi, *anþi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énti. Compare Dutch en, English and.

funFacts: The sign & is called das Kaufmanns-Und (“merchant's and”) in German.
pitfalls: und does not change the word order: … und sie deckt den Tisch (verb still second).
subtleties: No comma before und in a simple list (Tomaten, Gurken und Zwiebeln); between two full main clauses the comma is optional.

profile.feeling: The most frequent word of German: it carries gender, number and case of the noun.

senses.def: the (definite article): der (masc.), die (fem. and plural), das (neut.), with case forms den, dem, des, der
before names in colloquial southern German: der Peter, die Anna

examples.tr: Give the radish to the child.

collocations.text: im, am, zum (= in dem, an dem, zu dem)

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; the demonstratives dieser and the stressed der/die/das point more strongly.

etymology.text: From Middle High German dër, from Old High German dër, replacing the original masculine and feminine nominative forms from Proto-Germanic *sa by analogy with the adjective inflection. Cognate with Yiddish דער (der).

funFacts: The German Sesame Street theme song begins with the three articles: “Der, die, das …”.
pitfalls: Learn every noun with its article: the gender is often not predictable (der Kohl, die Gurke, das Radieschen).
die is feminine singular AND every plural; der is masculine nominative AND feminine dative/genitive AND genitive plural.
subtleties: Compounds take the article of their last part: der Kohl → der Blumenkohl; die Zwiebel → die Frühlingszwiebel.

profile.feeling: Something new to the conversation, or just one of many.

senses.def: a, an (indefinite article)
one (the numeral; stressed in speech)

examples.text: Ich nehme nur einen Kaffee, nicht zwei.
examples.tr: I'll just have one coffee, not two.

phrases.meaning: a promise is a promise

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; colloquially ein is shortened to 'n (Hast du 'n Stift?).

etymology.text: From Middle High German ein, from Old High German ein. Compare Dutch een, English one, Danish en.

funFacts: English a/an and one are the same word historically – just like German ein.
pitfalls: ein has no plural: a tomato = eine Tomate, tomatoes = Tomaten (no article).
Masculine accusative adds -en: Ich kaufe einen Kürbis.
subtleties: Its negative is kein: eine Tomate → keine Tomate.

profile.feeling: Pointing: this one here (or that one there) – clearer than the article.

senses.def: this (also: that) – points to a particular thing
dieser / diese / dieses alone: this one

examples.text: Welche Gurke willst du? – Diese hier.
examples.tr: Which cucumber do you want? – This one here.

synonyms.nuance: in speech the stressed article often replaces dieser: DIE Tomate (da)
that (far) – old-fashioned and written; contrasted with dieser

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German diser/dirre, disiu, diz, from Old High German dësēr, disiu, diz, from the Old High German demonstrative pronoun dër, from Proto-Germanic *sa, from Proto-Indo-European *tód.

funFacts: dieser has the same endings as der in all cases – -er, -e, -es, -en, -em – which is why it is often used to learn the article endings.
pitfalls: Neuter is dieses (dieses Radieschen), not *dieser; the short form dies is used mostly as a pronoun in writing (Dies ist …).
subtleties: German does not distinguish this/that sharply: dieser covers both; in speech people often say der da or das hier.

profile.feeling: The pointing word of “Das ist …” – used for anything you show or name.

senses.def: this, that (demonstrative pronoun): Das ist eine Tomate. Das sind Tomaten.
that (referring to a whole statement): Das weiß ich nicht.

phrases.meaning: that's all, we're finished

synonyms.nuance: short form of dieses; Dies ist … sounds written or formal

etymology.text: From Middle High German daȥ, from Old High German daȥ, from Proto-Germanic *þat. Compare Dutch dat, English that. Doublet of dass.

funFacts: das and dass (“that”, conjunction) are historically the same word; the spelling difference is only a convention.
pitfalls: In Das ist … the das never changes with the noun: Das ist ein Kürbis / eine Gurke / ein Radieschen; for plurals the verb changes: Das sind Gurken.
subtleties: This das is the neuter form of the demonstrative der/die/das; its dative is dem and its genitive dessen (not des).

profile.feeling: Curiosity – and, alone and sharp, a slightly rude “What?”.

senses.def: what? (interrogative pronoun)
what, which (relative: alles, was …)
something (= etwas, colloquial: Ich habe was gefunden)

examples.text: Alles, was du brauchst, ist im Kühlschrank.
examples.tr: Everything you need is in the fridge.
Do you want something to eat?

phrases.meaning: What's going on? / What's wrong?

synonyms.nuance: “Pardon?” – the polite way to ask someone to repeat; a bare Was? sounds rude

etymology.text: From Middle High German waȥ, from Old High German waȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷod. Cognate with Dutch wat, English what, Danish hvad.

funFacts: German w- question words match English wh- words: was – what, wo – where, wer – who (careful!).
pitfalls: False friend: German was = what, not the English past tense “was” (that is war).
After prepositions standard German uses wo(r)- + preposition: Womit? Worüber? – mit was is colloquial.
subtleties: Was? alone sounds abrupt; Wie bitte? is the polite version.

profile.feeling: Searching for something – the keys, the station, the garlic.

senses.def: where? (at what place)
where (relative: die Stadt, wo ich wohne)
somewhere (= irgendwo, colloquial)

examples.tr: Excuse me, where is the station?

examples.text: Das ist die Stadt, wo ich geboren bin.
examples.tr: That's the town where I was born.

examples.text: Ich habe meine Brille wo liegen lassen.

synonyms.nuance: at which place – stiff, written

etymology.text: With a widespread dialectal shift from -ā- to -ō-, from Middle High German wā, wār, from Old High German wār, hwār, from Proto-West Germanic *hwār, from Proto-Germanic *hwēr, *hwar; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís, whence also wer. Cognate with English where.

funFacts: The old -r of wo (compare English where) survives in compounds: woran, worauf, worin.
pitfalls: wo is only for location: wohin = where to (Wohin gehst du?), woher = where from (Woher kommst du?).
False friend: German wo = where, German wer = who.
subtleties: In southern German speech wo is also used as a relative pronoun (der Mann, wo …) – nonstandard.

profile.feeling: Right here, within reach – presence and attention.

senses.def: here (in this place)
here, at this point (in a text or discussion)
Hier! – “present!” (answer at roll call); also “here you are” when handing something

collocations.tr: here and there; now and then

phrases.meaning: in some places; from time to time

synonyms.nuance: in speech often means “here” as well as “there”: Ich bin da.
at this point – in writing and speeches

etymology.text: From Middle High German hier, from Old High German hier, from Proto-West Germanic *hēr. Cognate with Dutch hier, English here, Swedish här.

funFacts: In German schools and the army, pupils and soldiers answer the roll call with Hier!
pitfalls: For movement towards the speaker standard German uses her or hierher: Komm her! / Komm hierher!
subtleties: hier, da and dort: hier is close to the speaker, dort is far away, and da can be either.
